newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia inflation under control - economists.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia inflation under control - economists.

text.p: A rise of 3.5 percent in Malaysia's consumer price index last year showed inflation was within forecasts and under control, economists said on Thursday.

They said Malaysia would be able to continue keeping inflation under check this year with its well tested formula of maintaining high interest rates and a slower economic growth rate, which were now backed by a strengthening ringgit.
"I think the tight monetary policy and liberalisation of import duties has helped contain inflation," said Chung Tin Fah, head of research at OSK & Partners.
"Slower economic growth coupled with the strengthening of the ringgit should keep inflation below four percent this year," the economist said.
Malaysia's inflation rate, as measured by the consumer price index, was 3.4 percent year-on-year in 1995.
The Statistics Department said inflation in December was 3.3 percent year-on-year, the same as in November.
Rising food prices remained the biggest contributor. The food index grew by 5.7 percent in 1996, the department said.
"There are no surprises in the figures. We did not expect there to be any," said Fiona Leong, head of research at J.M. Sassoon & Co in Kuala Lumpur.

"The numbers are quite respectable and are unlikely to fuel sentiment either way. We had forecast a rate of 3.6 percent for 1996. For 1997, our forecast is 3.8 percent," said Patrick Tan, economist at brokers H.G. Asia in Kuala Lumpur.
In a poll by Reuters in December, 16 large research houses forecast an average 3.53 percent rise in CPI in 1997.
Economists have said the announced inflation rate may not be a complete trend indicator as prices of most items weighted in the CPI are controlled.
However, the CPI gave an indication of any underlying price pressure in the the economy, they said.

Inflationary pressures and a widening current account deficit in the fast-growing economy triggered worries about overheating last year and forced Malaysia to slow down growth and maintain high interest rates.
Malaysia's benchmark three-month interbank interest rate at around 7.3 percent is at least four percentage points higher than in neighbouring Singapore.
Malaysia has recorded a sharply lower trade deficit of 954.35 million ringgit ($378 million) in the first 10 months of 1996 against around 9.96 billion in the corresponding period of 1995.

Malaysia's 1996 gross domestic product growth is expected to have fallen to 8.2 percent, following 9.5 percent growth in 1995. The country has reported nine straight years of growth over eight percent, which is expected to be maintained until 2000.
In addition, the ringgit's rise of over two percent against the dollar in the last 10 days is expected to bring down the nation's import bill.
"With the strong ringgit and high interest rates, I don't see much room for inflation to rise," said an analyst with a Malaysian bank in Kuala Lumpur.
He said there may be some seasonal rise next month due to the Eid al-Fitr and Chinese Lunar New Year festivals. However, it would not affect the overall trend.
-- Kuala Lumpur newsroom (603-230 8911)
